chunks.title: Does this site track visitors?
chunks.text: There are no cookies, no analytics and no tracking scripts, and the site stores nothing about you on any server. One thing does leave your browser: when a page opens, it asks the free service api.ipify.org for your public IP address and shows it back to you in the address bar (for example /ip=203.0.113.9) and in the footer. This site does not store or log that address. It is kept only for the current browser session and is gone when you close the tab. If you would rather not use it, block api.ipify.org (for example with an ad blocker) and the site works the same without it.

chunks.title: What is the ip= part of the URL?
chunks.text: Your own public IP address, as reported by api.ipify.org when you opened the page. It is added to the address bar without reloading the page. Be aware that it is then part of the URL, so it appears in your browser history and in screenshots, and anyone you send that exact link to will see it. If someone opens a link that contains another person's address, the site replaces it at once with their own.

chunks.title: What is the loading screen at the start?
chunks.text: A short boot sequence that looks like a model loading its weights. Its progress bar follows real loading (fonts, the main script and the data files), it shows once per visit, and you can click or press any key to skip it.

chunks.title: Does the site change depending on who I am?
chunks.text: A little, and only in your browser. At the start it reads harmless context (time of day, device type, language, light or dark mode, where you came from, and whether you have visited before) and a simple hand-written rule set, not a trained model, guesses whether you are probably a recruiter, a developer, a researcher or just curious. It then adjusts the greeting, the order of the sections and the second button in the top section. The guess is only a heuristic and often says "curious" because many apps hide where a visit came from. You can correct it with "not you? switch" under the headline. The guess is worked out in your browser and kept only for the current browser session; the only thing that leaves your browser is the public IP lookup described above.

chunks.title: What does the loading animation show?
chunks.text: A small neural network doing one forward pass. Each pulse is a real file finishing loading (fonts, scripts, data, the portrait), the log lines carry real sizes and counts, and the greeting at the end is decoded token by token. At the end the network collapses into the first letters of the headline. It plays once per session, and you can click or press any key to skip it.

chunks.title: CrohnSight: overview
chunks.text: CrohnSight (Medical computer vision, 2026). Problem: Reading a capsule-endoscopy study means checking tens of thousands of small-bowel frames by eye. Crohn's lesions are small and easy to miss. Approach: An ensemble of 10 EfficientNet-B2 models (5 folds × 2 seeds) at the native 320 px finds lesions in 7 classes, grades severity in 4 tiers and draws a heat-map over each lesion. It is exported to ONNX and runs offline on an ordinary CPU. Add-ons cover ulcerative-colitis Mayo grading and flare-risk forecasting.

chunks.title: CrohnSight: results and stack
chunks.text: Key result: 0.992 AUROC, lesion vs normal (CrohnIPI). Lesion vs normal accuracy: 96.7% (best published 94.6%). Severity, quadratic weighted κ: 0.94. External test, Kvasir-Capsule: AUROC 0.944, no retraining. Stack: PyTorch, EfficientNet-B2, ONNX Runtime, FastAPI, Next.js, Docker. Research prototype, not a medical device. Telling a whole lesion video from a lesion-free one is near chance (study AUROC 0.57). The README reports this openly. With Hil Kalathiya and Chetan Gadhiya · PDEU minor project, guided by Prof. Dr. Babalu Kumar Singh. Code: https://github.com/SahajIVVIX-1/Crohn-Disease-Early-Prediction

chunks.title: CrohnSight README: Why
chunks.text: A capsule endoscopy study is tens of thousands of frames, and a gastroenterologist reads every one looking for lesions that can be a few millimetres wide. CrohnSight scores each frame, ranks a study so the most suspicious frames come first, grades severity on a four-step scale, and draws a heat-map so a reader can check why a frame was flagged. Two add-ons cover the rest of inflammatory bowel disease: an ulcerative colitis Mayo grader for colonoscopy images and a flare-risk forecaster for follow-up visits.

chunks.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator: overview
chunks.text: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator (Multi-agent LLM system, 2026). Problem: Enterprise questions mix document lookups, database queries and actions such as sending email. A single RAG chain answers them badly or unsafely. Approach: A LangGraph Supervisor → Worker → Validator graph routes each query to Corrective RAG, NL-to-SQL, a human-in-the-loop email tool or chat. Retrieval is hybrid (Qdrant dense + BM25), reranked with a CrossEncoder and expanded from 200- to 800-token parent chunks, with an LLM grader that rewrites weak queries. A semantic cache, prompt-injection guards and Fernet encryption protect it.

chunks.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator: results and stack
chunks.text: Key result: 0.81 RAGAS faithfulness. Context precision: 1.00. Context recall: 0.90. Answer relevancy: 0.75. Stack: LangGraph, LangChain, FastAPI, Qdrant, BM25, Redis, Next.js, RAGAS.  Solo project. Code: https://github.com/SahajIVVIX-1/Multi-Agent-RAG

chunks.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator README: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator
chunks.text: Developed by: Sahaj S. GitHub: @SahajIVVIX-1 Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator is a production-grade Multi-Agent Agentic RAG system designed for complex enterprise workflows. A Supervisor→Worker→Validator pipeline routes every query to the right specialist agent, with a LangGraph-powered Corrective RAG loop for high-fidelity retrieval and a strict human-in-the-loop protocol for external actions.

chunks.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator README: Resume & Portfolio Highlights
chunks.text: - Multi-Agent Orchestration : Designed a stateful Supervisor-Worker-Validator architecture utilizing LangGraph and LangChain to route queries among specialized agents (Corrective RAG, Natural Language to SQL, Human-in-the-Loop external tools, and Conversational agents). - Corrective RAG (CRAG) with LangGraph : Implemented a self-correcting retrieval graph that uses an LLM grader to evaluate document relevance, dynamically triggering query rewriting and re-retrieval (bounded to 2 iterations to prevent latency spikes). - Hybrid Retrieval & Hierarchical Context Expansion : Integrated 384-dimensional dense semantic vectors (Qdrant) and sparse keyword search (BM25) with CrossEncoder neural reranking ( ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 ) and parent-child chunk expansion (200-token retrieval units expanded to 800-token parent context).

chunks.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator README: Resume & Portfolio Highlights
chunks.text: - RAGAS Quality Benchmarking : Achieved 0.81 Faithfulness , 1.00 Context Precision , 0.90 Context Recall , and 0.75 Answer Relevancy across enterprise evaluation datasets. - Enterprise Security & Safeguards : Engineered a defense-in-depth security perimeter with constant-time two-tier API key authentication, IP-based sliding window rate limiting via Redis, regex-based prompt injection barriers, read-only SQLite/MySQL URI isolation, and symmetric Fernet encryption at rest for external credentials. - Human-in-the-Loop Protocol : Implemented a strict Draft → Confirm → Execute workflow for transactional operations (email actions) with domain allow-listing and hourly rate caps.

chunks.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator README: Resume & Portfolio Highlights
chunks.text: - High-Performance Caching : Designed an Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) semantic cache using Qdrant (cosine similarity ≥ 0.96) to deliver sub-millisecond responses on repeated semantic queries, backed by Redis for multi-tenant conversation session persistence.

chunks.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator README: 1. Supervisor  Worker  Validator Pipeline
chunks.text: An LLM Supervisor classifies every message into one of four routes: Route Agent Capability retriever RetrieverAgent Corrective RAG over company documents db DBAgent Natural-language SQL over company.db / MySQL tool ToolAgent Email with Draft → Confirm → Execute HitL chat ChatAgent Conversational follow-ups and greetings Every agent output passes through a Validation Agent that re-grounds and normalises the answer into {answer, source, confidence} before returning to the caller.

chunks.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator README: 2. Corrective RAG Loop (LangGraph)
chunks.text: RetrieverAgent implements a self-correcting retrieval graph: - Grader : LLM scores each retrieved document as relevant/irrelevant; fail-opens on error. - Rewriter : rewrites the query to be more search-friendly before retrying. - Max 2 iterations to bound latency.

chunks.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator README: 3. Parent-Child Chunking
chunks.text: Documents are split at two granularities: Level Size Purpose Child chunks 200 tokens Stored in Qdrant — precise semantic retrieval Parent chunks 800 tokens Stored in ParentStore (JSON) — richer LLM context After reranking, each retrieved child is swapped for its parent text before being passed to the answer LLM.

chunks.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator README: 4. Hybrid Retrieval
chunks.text: CompanyRetriever runs a 5-stage pipeline on every query: 1. Query rewrite — LLM expands the query (acronyms, keywords) 2. Dense search — Qdrant similarity search (top retriever top k × 4 ) 3. Sparse search — BM25 over the same corpus 4. CrossEncoder rerank — cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 scores all candidates; top retriever top k kept 5. Parent expansion — child chunks replaced with their 800-token parents

chunks.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator README: 5. Security
chunks.text: - Two-tier auth : X-API-Key or Authorization: Bearer — require identity for /chat , require admin for /settings , /upload , /documents - Prompt injection guard : 8-pattern substring check at the /chat boundary - SQL lockdown : read-only SQLite URI ( mode=ro ), user settings table hidden from the SQL agent - Upload sanitisation : os.path.basename , extension allow-list, 20 MB size cap - Email guardrails : domain allow-list, hourly send cap, Draft → Confirm → Execute protocol - Secret masking : /settings GET returns " set " — never decrypts to caller - Rate limiting : Redis INCR keyed on source IP, 10 req/min default

chunks.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG Orchestrator README: 6. Scalability
chunks.text: - Semantic cache : Qdrant ANN lookup; cosine similarity ≥ 0.96 skips the full pipeline - Redis-backed indexing queue : INDEXING QUEUE is a Redis set ( orchestrator:indexing queue ) — safe across multiple workers - Qdrant lock safety : retriever releases the file lock ( client.close() ) before background re-indexing runs - Pooled Redis client : single connection reused across rate-limit and queue helpers

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent: overview
chunks.text: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent (Reinforcement learning environment, 2026). Problem: Cleaning a messy table takes many small, ordered decisions. Can an agent learn them, and can its score be checked honestly? Approach: An OpenEnv environment over pandas tables with reproducible (task, seed) episodes and a hidden clean ground truth. Potential-based reward shaping makes going in circles worthless, and a separate grader scores the final table. The benchmark compares a PPO agent (400k steps, exported to NumPy), a zero-shot Llama 3.1 8B agent and rule-based baselines, served over FastAPI and WebSocket with a Gradio demo.

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent: results and stack
chunks.text: Key result: 0.967 PPO grader score on hard-clean. Improvement over doing nothing: +0.917 on hard-clean. Invalid-action rate (PPO): 0.0%. Llama 3.1 8B zero-shot: 0.838 on hard-clean. Stack: OpenEnv, Stable-Baselines3 PPO, Llama 3.1 8B, Pydantic, FastAPI, Docker, HF Spaces. The data is synthetic, and Q is only a proxy for quality, which is why a separate grader exists. With Chetan Gadhiya and Hil Kalathiya. Code: https://github.com/SahajIVVIX-1/open-env-nuclei

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent README: OpenEnv Data Cleaning Environment
chunks.text: An OpenEnv environment where an agent cleans a dirty pandas table one action at a time, plus baselines, a benchmark, an LLM agent and a Gradio demo. - Reproducible: every episode is (task id, seed) - the same dirty table, with a hidden clean ground truth. - Honest scoring: the training-style reward and the final grader score are separate things (see below). - Agents included: do-nothing, random, a rule-based heuristic, a trained RL agent (PPO), and a zero-shot LLM agent (Llama 3.1 8B through the Hugging Face router).

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent README: OpenEnv Data Cleaning Environment
chunks.text: The RL agent is trained with PPO on held-out seeds and runs via lightweight pure-NumPy inference with zero PyTorch dependencies at runtime. The Hugging Face Space demo runs at chetangadhiya017-data-cleaning-env.hf.space. To redeploy the latest code, see Deploy.

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent README: How it works
chunks.text: Episode: reset(task id, seed) - repeat step(action) - finish (or the step budget runs out).

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent README: Tasks
chunks.text: Task Rows Step budget What is wrong with the data easy-clean 40 15 missing values in age , monthly spend , and plan medium-clean 60 (+duplicates) 25 missing values in four columns and 15% exact duplicate rows hard-clean 100 (+duplicates) 45 all of the above plus inconsistent categories ( NY , new york , New York ), numbers stored as text ( "25" ), N/A placeholders, impossible values (age 999), mixed date formats, stray whitespace The table is a synthetic customers table: customer id, name, age, city, signup date, plan, monthly spend .

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent README: Actions
chunks.text: action type Fields Effect fill missing column name , strategy ( mean / median / mode / constant ), value (constant only) fill nulls drop duplicates - remove exact duplicate rows standardize categories column name , optional mapping fix case/spacing; map aliases like NY - New York cast type column name , target type ( int / float / str ) convert text to numbers (placeholders become nulls) strip whitespace optional column name trim and collapse spaces fix dates column name normalise mixed formats to YYYY-MM-DD clip outliers column name clip to the column's valid range drop rows with missing optional column name drop rows with nulls (penalised: loses data) finish - end the episode Invalid actions (unknown column, mean on text, a string constant in a numeric column, ...) are not applied ; the agent receives an explanation in last error and a small penalty.

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent README: Observation
chunks.text: task id, seed, row count, duplicate count, total missing, step count, steps remaining, quality score, total reward, invalid action count, last action, last action ok, last message, last error, data sample (first 5 rows) and one column profile per column: dtype, expected type, missing, unique, sample values, issues (e.g. {"missing": 5, "whitespace": 3} ), allowed values , bad values , valid range . The expected types, allowed category values and valid ranges are part of the task description, like constraints in a database schema. final score and score breakdown are null until the episode is over.

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent README: Reward
chunks.text: Q is an observable quality score: Q = 1 - (schema violations + duplicate rows n columns) / (initial rows n columns) . The progress terms add up to 10 (Q end - Q start) , so repeating actions or going in circles cannot earn reward (there is a test for this). observation.reward is the reward of the last step only; total reward is the sum.

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent README: Grader (separate from the reward)
chunks.text: score = 0.6 cell accuracy + 0.2 row fidelity + 0.2 schema score , in [0, 1], computed against the hidden ground truth and revealed only in the final observation. Numeric cells earn partial credit by closeness (an imputed value is never exactly right); a table identical to the ground truth scores exactly 1.0. Because imputation is approximate, the best realistic score is below 1.0 even when Q reaches 1.0.

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent README: RL Training & Learning Curve
chunks.text: The RL agent was trained for 400,000 steps using Stable-Baselines3 PPO across 8 parallel environment workers ( SubprocVecEnv ), evaluated every 20,480 steps on held-out validation seeds 50–59, and benchmarked on held-out test seeds 0–9 (which were never exposed during training). Weights are saved as models/ppo policy.npz (and metadata in models/ppo policy.json ). Key learning insights: - Zero invalid actions: The policy learned to never issue invalid actions across any task or test seed (0.0% invalid-action rate). - Matched heuristic performance: On hard-clean , PPO learned to reach 0.967 ± 0.004 (+0.917 improvement) , virtually identical to the hand-crafted rule-based agent ( 0.968 ± 0.003 (+0.918 improvement) ).

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent README: RL Training & Learning Curve
chunks.text: - Proper operation sequencing: PPO learned to strip whitespace and standardise categories before handling missing values, avoided destructive row drops, and called finish once high quality was attained. - Lightweight deployment: The policy is exported to NumPy arrays and runs with zero PyTorch dependencies on CPU in the Space demo.

chunks.title: OpenEnv Data-Cleaning Agent README: Limitations
chunks.text: - The data is synthetic; results do not transfer to real data automatically. - Q is a proxy for quality: an agent can raise Q with a bad imputation (e.g. a constant). The grader exists to catch such gaps. - Only one grader weighting and one noise model are implemented. - Action-space engineering: the RL agent's standardize aliases:city action is a macro that generates alias mappings using the rule-based heuristic, so the policy learns when to execute the transformation rather than discovering arbitrary character mappings from scratch.

chunks.title: Sleep-Consolidating LLM: overview
chunks.text: Sleep-Consolidating LLM (Continual-learning research, 2026). Problem: A language model learns nothing from what happens after training. An agent can keep notes, but the model itself either never absorbs them or, once fine-tuned on them, forgets older skills. Can it "sleep": turn a day's notes into weights without losing what it already knew? Approach: Each simulated day a 4-bit Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct reads documents from a seeded synthetic world of names it cannot know (about 20% of facts are later updated) and writes atomic notes. At night it dreams: grounded question-answer pairs (answer-first), paraphrases and counterfactuals, de-duplicated and selected for diversity. One rank-16 QLoRA adapter is trained on a mix of 40% dreams from earlier nights, 20% ARC-Easy, HellaSwag and GSM8K train items and 40% new dreams, with a KL-to-base penalty on the replay part. QA is scored on held-out phrasings with no notebook.

chunks.title: Sleep-Consolidating LLM: results and stack
chunks.text: Key result: 0.325 recall of earlier days' facts after 5 nights, no notebook (naive training: 0.035). Today's facts, held-out phrasings: 0.38 (naive 0.11), mean of 3 seeds. Old-skill probe (ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, GSM8K): 0.475 (base model 0.460, naive 0.392). WikiText-2 perplexity: 39.6 (base model 26.6, naive 44.2). Hardware: 4 GB laptop GPU (RTX 3050), 4-bit base model. Stack: PyTorch, Qwen2.5-0.5B, QLoRA (NF4), PEFT, bitsandbytes, Transformers, pytest. Indicative only: 3 seeds, 5 nights, a 0.5B model and roughly 50 to 100 questions per cell. Training on dreams at all raises perplexity above the base model. Whether one rank-16 adapter holds about 1,500 facts is untested; a 30-night run is in progress. The earlier replay design forgot most earlier days (0.07 at day 5). Solo project. Code: https://github.com/SahajIVVIX-1/Sleep-Consolidating-LLM

chunks.title: Sleep-Consolidating LLM README: Sleep-Consolidating LLM
chunks.text: Can a language model learn from its day the way a brain does: take notes while awake, then "sleep" and turn the notes into weights, without forgetting what it already knew? This project builds that loop on a laptop with a 4 GB GPU and measures it honestly.

chunks.title: Sleep-Consolidating LLM README: The loop
chunks.text: Each simulated day has a day phase and a night phase. - Day. A 4-bit Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct reads that day's documents and writes atomic fact notes into an append-only notebook. Notes are scored against the ground truth of the world (day 1: 41 of 50 sentences parsed, recall 0.70, precision 0.85). - Night. The model dreams. From the notes it generates question-answer pairs, paraphrases and counterfactual variations, then trains one QLoRA adapter on them mixed with replay. - Morning. Questions about the new facts are asked with no notebook access, so only what reached the weights counts.

chunks.title: Sleep-Consolidating LLM README: Synthetic world
chunks.text: Names of people, companies, cities and products are built from syllable generators so the base model has no prior (measured accuracy before the night: 0.000). Each day adds 20 to 50 facts as (subject, relation, object) triples, and about 20% from day 2 on update earlier facts, so "latest value wins" can be checked. Question templates are split into train templates (the dream generator may use them) and held-out templates (never shown to the generator or the trainer); a unit test enforces the split.

chunks.title: Sleep-Consolidating LLM README: Dreams
chunks.text: - Answer-first QA. The answer is the extracted object of the note and the model only writes the question. This raised the share of valid dream questions from 19% to 69% on the first pass. - Grounding and de-duplication. The question must mention the subject, must not contain the answer and must end with a question mark; near-duplicates (cosine above 0.92) are dropped. - Diversity regulariser. Candidates are over-generated 3 times, then chosen by greedy max-min selection with per-fact coverage and per-kind quotas (QA, paraphrase, counterfactual, multi-hop). Distinct-n, self-BLEU and MiniLM embedding dispersion are logged every night, and a collapse alarm raises the sampling temperature.

chunks.title: Sleep-Consolidating LLM README: Sleep
chunks.text: - QLoRA. NF4 with double quantisation, rank 16, alpha 32, all linear projections, gradient checkpointing, micro-batch 2, sequence length 256. Loss is on answer tokens only. - Replay. A night mixes 40% dreams from earlier nights (a day-balanced reservoir, counterfactuals excluded, dreams of superseded facts pruned), 20% old-skill items from the ARC-Easy, HellaSwag and GSM8K train splits and 40% new dreams. - KL to the base model. A KL penalty on the replay tokens keeps the language distribution from drifting; weights 0.1 and 0.2 were tried. - One adapter. A single adapter is trained continuously across nights.

chunks.title: Sleep-Consolidating LLM README: Sleep
chunks.text: Merging into a 4-bit base is lossy and costs RAM on a 4 GB card. - Lean logits. The language-model head is evaluated only at assistant-token positions. This fixed a replay-only memory spike (peak RSS 5.0 GB to 1.8 GB) caused by the batch x sequence x 152k fp32 logits tensor spilling into system RAM, with the same loss and gradients.

chunks.title: Sleep-Consolidating LLM README: Evaluation

chunks.title: Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation: overview
chunks.text: Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation (Kaggle competition · quantum compilation, 2026). Problem: Fault-tolerant quantum algorithms are priced in qubits and Toffoli gates. Google Quantum AI's Kaggle competition asks for smaller circuits for three workloads: a 1/√x phase for fusion energy, a Reed-Solomon decoder for optimisation and FeMoCo chemistry loaders. An official verifier checks every submission on fresh random inputs, and the score is the geometric mean of the three cost reductions. Approach: Own circuits for two of the three tasks, built with kickmix and checked with the official verifier logic. invsqrt: a table-based piecewise-quadratic design (192-entry QROM, binary shift count, barrel normaliser), lazy register allocation, narrow-window multiplies, measurement-based lookup erase and dead-gate removal checked over all 3.13M inputs. dqi: a tower-field GF(2^12) inverse (315 to 91 Toffolis), a 54-AND multiplier and a statistical dead-gate remover. Multi-core verifier runners for Windows run the full checks.

chunks.title: Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation: results and stack
chunks.text: Key result: 6.43× lower cost on invsqrt, own circuit (2,076,774 → 323,146). invsqrt, own v6: 136 qubits, 2,125 Toffolis; full 64-shot check on all 3.13M inputs passed. dqi, own v5: 1.64× (1,869 qubits; about 30 failures in 102,400 shots, R 1.276). Own composite: about 2.2 (6.43 × 1.64 × 1.0 for chemistry); not submitted. Own package scored on Kaggle: 1.628 (invsqrt v2 only), as predicted locally. Stack: Python, kickmix, Qualtran, NumPy, GF(2^12) tower fields, Kaggle. The leaderboard's top scores come from public circuits of other participants. Re-verifying and submitting one such public stack scored 33.17 on Kaggle, but that is their work, credited in the repo, not mine. My own circuits reach about 2.2 and the chemistry task is untouched (1.0×). The dqi figure depends on a few decoder failures that vary with the grader's random draw. The code is not public. Solo entry · public work of other participants credited. Competition page: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation

chunks.title: Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation README: Google Quantum AI Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation
chunks.text: Entry in the Kaggle competition Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation. The task is to shrink three fault-tolerant quantum circuits. Every submission is checked by official verifier scripts on fresh random inputs seeded by a hash of the submission, so there is no fixed hidden test set.

chunks.title: Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation README: Scoring
chunks.text: The score is the geometric mean of three cost reductions against the reference submission, which scores exactly 1.0. Task Workload Cost to minimise invsqrt fusion energy: phase e^(2 pi i/sqrt(x)) for x up to 3,133,452 qubits x (Toffolis + T/4) dqi optimisation: reversible Reed-Solomon RS(4095, 4025) decoder over GF(2^12) R(eps+) x Q^2 x T, failures allowed but priced dfthcsos chemistry: FeMoCo block encoding with QROM angle loaders lambda eff x T x Q

chunks.title: Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation README: invsqrt own design, 6.43x
chunks.text: The reference does a Quake-style initial guess plus a Newton step (260 qubits, 7,735 Toffolis, cost 2,076,774). The own circuits replace it step by step, each verified with the official logic on all 3,133,452 inputs. - Table-based piecewise quadratic. Normalise, look up three coefficients in a 192-entry QROM addressed by 8 bits, then two multiplies. Binary shift count with a barrel normaliser instead of thermometer flags: 4.31x. - Lazy register allocation. The y1, a2 and r registers are allocated only after normalisation and the multiplier scratch borrows idle qubits: Q 156 to 146, 4.61x. - Narrow-window multiplies.

chunks.title: Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation README: invsqrt own design, 6.43x
chunks.text: Each multiply row subtracts into an (n+1)-bit window whose top bit is the borrow, with window widths taken from the exact maxima over all inputs: Q 136, 5.44x. - Measurement-based lookup erase. The uncompute pass erases the loaded table entry with a measurement-based delete (about 25 Toffolis) instead of repeating the unary-iteration QROM (191): 5.78x. - Exhaustive dead-gate removal. A bit-parallel simulation over all inputs with random measurement outcomes found 267 Toffoli-like gates that are dead or have an implied control; removing them gives 136 qubits, 2,125 Toffolis, cost 323,146, 6.43x. The full 64-shot check (200,540,928 shots) passed.

chunks.title: Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation README: dqi own design, 1.64x
chunks.text: - Tower-field inversion. GF(2^12) as a tower over GF(2^6) turns the 315-Toffoli inverse into 91, tested exhaustively on all 4096 inputs, with erasure by measurement. - 54-AND multiplier. Karatsuba 12 = 2 x 6, 6 = 2 x 3 plus a solved linear reduction (66 with a quantum control instead of 75). - Statistical dead-gate removal. A bit-parallel simulation of the 73.9M-operation decoder over about 850k sampled shots deletes gates that never matter. This is statistical: rare shots become decoder failures (about 30 in 102,400), which raises R from 1.191 to 1.276 but lowers the total cost.

chunks.title: Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation README: Tooling
chunks.text: Multi-core verifier runners for Windows (the official ones fork-parallelise only), a circuit liveness and interval-colouring pass, a peephole analyser, a chemistry shape sweep and a composite-score helper. The full invsqrt check takes about 25 minutes on 16 cores.

chunks.title: Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation README: What is mine and what is not
chunks.text: My own circuits reach a composite of about 2.2 (6.43 x 1.64 x 1.0, chemistry untouched), and the own-code package scored 1.628 on Kaggle when only invsqrt v2 was submitted. The public leaderboard's top scores come from circuits other participants published; I re-verified one such public stack locally and it scored 33.17 on Kaggle, as predicted, but it is their work and is credited in the repo's provenance file.

chunks.title: Verifiable Quantum Circuit Compilation README: Findings kept honest
chunks.text: Bit-width trimming of the reference is exhausted. Cutting the per-position 12-bit zero tests in the public decoder fails because of false roots, and the public circuits have no free qubit to remove. Multi-x gains need a new algorithm per task, not parameter tuning.

chunks.title: Santa 2026: Elf Calculator: overview
chunks.text: Santa 2026: Elf Calculator (Kaggle competition · program synthesis, 2026). Problem: For each of 1,000 puzzles a calculator with 48 registers starts from a few numbers and must produce every one of several huge targets (up to about 10^18) using + − × and exact division. The score is the total number of instructions across all puzzles, lower is better. The sample submission needs 1,490,379. Approach: An exact referee re-implements the rules and replays every program. A Horner-style solver gives the baseline. A forward/backward dictionary beam search (meet-in-the-middle over 2 to 4M values), a value-DAG local search with register allocation and a C++ cone re-synthesiser then look for shorter programs, and a best-of merger replays banks of programs and keeps the shortest valid one per puzzle. A gap report shows about 80% of instructions build helper values and targets are mostly helper-op-helper.

chunks.title: Santa 2026: Elf Calculator: results and stack
chunks.text: Key result: 128,494 total instructions after merging public programs (sample: 1,490,379). Own Horner baseline: 629,025 (−58% vs the sample). Merged with public program banks: 133,610, then 128,494 with newer public outputs. Own search after the baseline: 0 instructions saved (beam, DAG search, cone re-synthesis up to 4 helpers). Trivial lower bound: 26,898. Stack: Python, C++, NumPy, pytest, Kaggle. Nearly all of the gain over my own baseline comes from other participants' public programs, replayed through the exact referee and credited in the repo; my beam search, local search and cone re-synthesis found nothing shorter than the public frontier. The code is in a private repository. Solo entry · public programs of other participants credited. Competition page: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/santa-2026

chunks.title: Santa 2026: Elf Calculator README: Santa 2026 The Elf Calculator
chunks.text: Entry in the Kaggle competition Santa 2026 - The Elf Calculator. Each of 1,000 puzzles gives a few starting values in registers and several target numbers. A program is a list of instructions [op, i, j, d] meaning rd = ri op rj on 48 registers with + - / (exact division). A target counts as soon as it appears in any register, and the score is the total number of instructions, so lower is better. Targets reach about 10^18 and each puzzle has its own value limit (up to 60 bits).

chunks.title: Santa 2026: Elf Calculator README: Engine
chunks.text: - Referee. referee.py re-implements the rules exactly (register bounds, exact division, the value limit) and replays every program. Nothing is trusted that the referee has not replayed. - Horner baseline. A Horner-style solver gives a valid program for every puzzle: 629,025 instructions against 1,490,379 for the sample submission. - Beam search. A forward dictionary of 2 to 4 million values, backward meet-in-the-middle lookups, a layered beam, register allocation and a resumable multiprocess cache. It is correct and referee-verified, but random targets are far from the start values and need about five hidden-program operations, so a 2M-value dictionary almost never hits them. - Value-DAG local search.

chunks.title: Santa 2026: Elf Calculator README: Engine
chunks.text: Reduce and shuffle moves on the dependency DAG of a program, followed by register allocation. - Cone re-synthesis. A C++ search that re-synthesises the cone of values behind a target with up to 4 helpers and 1.5M nodes. - Best-of merge. merge.py replays banks of programs and keeps the shortest valid one for every puzzle. Programs are parsed as data and replayed; nothing from other participants' repositories is executed.

chunks.title: Santa 2026: Elf Calculator README: Where the length is
chunks.text: A gap report over the final programs shows 724 independent random puzzles at 5.05 instructions per target (81.5% of all instructions), 223 multiplicative puzzles at 3.92, and clustered and tiny puzzles near 2.8. About 80% of instructions build helper values and targets are almost always helper-op-helper. The trivial lower bound (one instruction per target) is 26,898.

chunks.title: Santa 2026: Elf Calculator README: Progress
chunks.text: Round What Total : 0 sample submission 1,490,379 1 own Horner baseline 629,025 2 merge of public program banks 133,610 3 public Kaggle datasets and notebook outputs 128,505 4 to 5 own DAG local search and cone re-synthesis on all 1,000 puzzles 128,505 6 to 9 refreshes of public programs, further cone runs 128,494

chunks.title: Santa 2026: Elf Calculator README: Honest reading
chunks.text: Of the gain over my own baseline, essentially all comes from public programs of other participants, replayed through the exact referee and credited in the repository's notice file. My own search found no shorter program than the public frontier: one of 4,337 helpers was removable by re-derivation and cone swaps gave 744 equal-length alternatives and no savings. The loop stopped when its rate of gain fell far below the stopping rule.

chunks.text: src/santa26/ has the IO, referee, merge, DAG optimiser, cone search and the solvers, native/cone.cpp is the C++ cone search, scripts/ has scoring, merging, analysis and refresh scripts, and tests/ has pytest tests for the referee, beam search and optimiser. The repository is private.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+: overview
chunks.text: DCGAN Reproducibility+ (Generative vision research, 2026). Problem: The 2015 DCGAN is famously unstable, and most re-implementations show only a grid of blurry samples, never what the networks learned inside. Approach: Keeps Radford et al.'s all-convolutional architecture but swaps in an LSGAN loss, Spectral Normalization, a Xavier/Kaiming initialisation, discriminator dropout and label smoothing. A custom GANAnalyzer hooks into the layers to show learned filters, mid-layer feature maps and the separation of D(x) from D(G(z)).

chunks.text: Key result: 5 stability fixes over the 2015 paper, each documented. Dataset: CIFAR-10, 25 epochs. Diagnostics: Filters, feature maps, D(x) vs D(G(z)) histograms. Baseline: Radford et al., arXiv 1511.06434. Stack: PyTorch, LSGAN, Spectral Norm, Matplotlib, Jupyter.  Solo project. Code: https://github.com/SahajIVVIX-1/Modern-DCGAN-Reproducibility

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: Deep DCGAN Reproducibility Study Architecture & Analytics
chunks.text: A research-centric implementation of the DCGAN paper (Radford et al., 2015), modernized with 2018-2022 stability techniques and a professional post-training analytics pipeline.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: The Vision
chunks.text: This project isn't just about training another GAN—it's about understanding it. While most implementations just show you a grid of fuzzy images, this study dives deep into the "black box" of the Generator and Discriminator to visualize exactly how latent vectors become features.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: Key Highlights
chunks.text: Modern Stability : Upgraded the 2015 baseline with LSGAN (Least Squares) and Spectral Normalization to prevent the dreaded "vanishing gradient" problem. Deep Diagnostics : A custom GANAnalyzer class that hooks into the model's internal layers to visualize learned filters and feature maps without needing to retrain. High-Fidelity Evaluation : Automated 4-panel dashboarding for immediate assessments of model convergence and Nash Equilibrium.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: DCGAN Reproducibility Study Paper vs. Modern Implementation
chunks.text: A formal comparison between the baseline architecture proposed by Radford et al. (2015) and this enhanced, high-stability version for facial/object generation.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: Executive Summary
chunks.text: While this project replicates the All-Convolutional architecture and upsampling strategy defined in the 2015 paper, it adopts several modern training paradigms discovered between 2017 and 2020. These enhancements collectively solve the "instability" and "mode collapse" issues inherent in the original BCE-based GANs.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: 1. Mathematical and Architectural Comparison
chunks.text: Component Radford et al. (1511.06434) My Implementation (2026) Technical Rationale : : : : Loss Function Binary Cross Entropy (BCE) Least Squares GAN (LSGAN) BCE suffers from vanishing gradients when the D is too strong. LSGAN (Mean Squared Error) forces the G to generate data closer to the decision boundary even when it's already "passing." D Normalization Batch Normalization Spectral Normalization Spectral Norm enforces a Lipschitz constant of 1, providing a mathematical guarantee against the Discriminator's gradients exploding—crucial for high-res stability. Weight Init Normal(0, 0.02) Modern Xavier/Kaiming Hybrid Faster convergence and better flow of gradients through deep strided convolutions.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: 1. Mathematical and Architectural Comparison
chunks.text: Regularization None D-Dropout (0.3) Prevents the Discriminator from "overfitting" on the real dataset, which often causes the Generator to fail mid-training. Labels Hard Labels [0, 1] Label Smoothing [0.1, 0.9] Softens the target for the Discriminator to prevent it from becoming "too confident," which helps maintain gradient flow for the Generator.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: 2. Analytical Core (The Research Layer)
chunks.text: The original paper relied heavily on simple grid visualizations. This implementation introduces a dedicated GANAnalyzer framework that mirrors paper's Figure 5 but expands it with professional metrics.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: Fig 5 Filter Visualization
chunks.text: Original Paper : Visualized 128 randomized filters of the G's projection layer. This Project : Extracts and plots the RGB-channel filters of the first D layer, showing exactly what edge/texture detectors the model learned during the 25-epoch CIFAR-10 run.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: Modern Dashboards (Not in Paper)
chunks.text: Precision-Recall Histograms : Overlapping probability distributions ($D(x)$ vs $D(G(z))$) are used here to detect Mode Collapse before it happens—a diagnostic tool not available in 2015. Feature Map Hooks : We use PyTorch hooks to visualize the "intent" of the generator in mid-layer (e.g., at 16x16 resolution), providing a peek into how a low-dim latent vector becomes a high-dim image.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: 3. Conclusions for Reproducers
chunks.text: If we were to strictly follow the 1511.06434 paper, we would likely encounter the "jittering" loss common in early GAN research. By replacing the loss function with LSGAN and adding Spectral Normalization, we have successfully modernized the 2015 architecture to perform with 2026 levels of stability and detail.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: Comparison Paper vs. Reality
chunks.text: The original 2015 DCGAN was ground-breaking but famously unstable. This repository serves as a Reproducibility+ study. I've kept the original "All-Convolutional" architecture but swapped the underlying "engine" for something more robust. Wait... what exactly is different? I’ve documented every architectural shift from the 2015 paper to this implementation. Check out the Deep Paper Comparison for the full breakdown of why these changes were made.

chunks.title: DCGAN Reproducibility+ README: Analytics & Interpretation
chunks.text: The power of this repo lies in its post-training suite . You don't need to retrain the model to see what's happening inside: 1. Filter Visualization : Directly extract the Discriminator's "eyes" to see what edges/textures it is looking for. 2. Activation Maps : Hook into any ConvTranspose2d layer in the Generator to see "pre-images"—the fuzzy shapes the model builds before the final output. 3. Confidence Histograms : Plot $D(x)$ vs $D(G(z))$ score distributions to see exactly how well the model separates real from fake.

chunks.title: Smaran: overview
chunks.text: Smaran (Windows desktop app, 2026). Problem: Reminder apps either shout at you or hide in a calendar, and Windows' Task Scheduler is too heavy for everyday routines. People want to type "stretch every 45 min" or "call mom at 6pm", be nudged calmly, and have their PC do the dull things (lock, sleep, open a file) on its own. Approach: A tray app that parses plain sentences into schedules and slides in a small card with Done and Snooze. Normal reminders fade away; important ones stay and break through quiet hours and full-screen apps. Automations chain up to 20 steps (open apps, files, scripts and links, or lock, sleep, sign out, shut down) on a time or a Windows event, with a 30-second cancellable countdown before anything destructive. Licences are Ed25519-signed cards hidden in a PNG and checked offline.

chunks.title: vMix Manager: overview
chunks.text: vMix Manager (Desktop production tool, 2026). Problem: Large live shows have hundreds of playback files, and vMix's own interface means dragging them in one by one, renaming categories by hand and fixing broken paths input by input, hours before going on air. Approach: Instead of controlling vMix through its API, it edits the .vmix session file's XML directly, so nothing needs to be open. Batch import queues folders and puts a bold GT Title divider before each one; a deep swap physically moves inputs between category slots while keeping their order; clone and relink checks every path (found or missing) and rebases a whole project onto a new drive; three wipe levels and drag-and-drop reordering finish the job. Every cloned input gets a fresh UUID.

chunks.title: vMix Manager: results and stack
chunks.text: Key result: XML edits .vmix session files directly, no running vMix needed. Interface: PyQt6, high-contrast black and white with Cambria type for stressful shows. Batch import: many folders queued, one GT Title header injected per folder. Category swap: rewrites each input's category and keeps its position order. Safety: fresh UUID per cloned input; the README says to back up .vmix files first. Stack: Python, PyQt6, XML, PyInstaller, vMix 24+. An independent tool, not affiliated with or endorsed by StudioCoast (vMix). It rewrites session files directly, so a backup before any bulk operation is essential. Built for Windows and vMix 24 or newer. Solo product. Code: https://github.com/SahajIVVIX-1/vMix-Manager

chunks.title: vMix Manager README: Direct XML Production Engine & Batch Automation Suite
chunks.text: vMix Manager is a specialized production utility designed for engineers who manage large-scale vMix sessions. Unlike the standard vMix interface, which requires manual input-by-input adjustments, vMix Manager operates directly on the .vmix XML schema. This allows for near-instantaneous batch operations, category migrations, and asset relinking that are impossible within the native vMix GUI.

chunks.title: vMix Manager README: Design Philosophy
chunks.text: vMix Manager features a Professional High-Contrast interface utilizing the Cambria typography stack. The UI is designed for high-stress production environments, focusing on readability, minimal distraction (Pure Black & White), and robust activity logging.

chunks.title: vMix Manager README: 1. Direct XML Manipulation Engine
chunks.text: The software does not "control" vMix via API; instead, it parses the underlying XML structure of a .vmix file. Offline Editing: Modify production files without having vMix open or consuming CPU/GPU resources. GUID Integrity: Every cloned or imported input is assigned a fresh UUID , preventing "Key Collision" errors when vMix loads the file. Attribute Preservation: All metadata including Volume, Mute states, Loop settings, and Position coordinates are preserved during category swaps.

chunks.title: vMix Manager README: 2. Smart Folder Inhalation (Batch Import)
chunks.text: Designed for shows with hundreds of playback assets. Multi-Queueing: Add dozens of folders to a staging list. Automated Header Injection: For every folder imported, the engine automatically creates a GT Title Divider . XML Payload Injection: It injects a custom XML payload into the GT Title to force a 214px Bold Arial font targeting the Message.Text field, ensuring dividers are visible on multiviewers. Template Path: Automatically targets the native vMix path: C:\Program Files (x86)\vMix\titles\GT Text\Text Middle Centre Left Right Sharp.gtzip .

chunks.title: vMix Manager README: 3. Category Interchanger (The Deep Swap)
chunks.text: Standard vMix only allows renaming categories. vMix Manager allows you to physically move content between slots. Slot Mapping: Supports the standard vMix architecture (Slots 1–6 and Custom Slots 50–65). The Swap Logic: When swapping Category A and Category B, the engine iterates through all Input objects and rewrites their Category attribute while maintaining their internal Position order.

chunks.title: vMix Manager README: 4. Category Cloning & Relinking
chunks.text: Import structures from existing .vmix files or folder trees. Status Verification: Automatically scans paths and marks assets with ✅ (Found) or ❌ (Missing). Root Relinking: If a project has moved to a different drive, use "Relink Root" to batch-update all file paths to a new directory while keeping the category structure intact.

chunks.text: Feature Description Use Case : : : Header Title Gen Injects GT Titles as dividers between folder batches. Organizing a 4-hour awards show with 20 categories. Factory Export Copies all physical files from a category into a new folder on disk. Consolidating assets for a backup machine or external editor. Wipe Logic Three tiers: Clear Category, Wipe All Inputs, or Factory Reset. Preparing a "Daily Clean" session from a complex template. Drag-Drop Reorder Manually reorder inputs in a table and save the new XML sequence. Sorting playback items without fighting the vMix GUI scroll. chunks.title: vMix Manager README: Usage Guide
chunks.text: 1. Open Session: Load your .vmix file via File Open . 2. Organize Categories: Use the sidebar to rename categories. Right-click to reset slots to "Empty Cat". 3. Batch Import: Go to Folder Import . Add your "Stingers," "VTs," and "Sponsors" folders. Click "Start Bulk Import." Each group will appear in your current category separated by high-visibility text headers. 4. Transform: Use the Transform tab to swap your "Red" category with "Custom 10" instantly. 5. Save: Save the file and open it in vMix. All inputs will appear exactly as structured.

chunks.title: SentinelProxy Suite: overview
chunks.text: SentinelProxy Suite (Local network security tool, 2026). Problem: Ad and tracker blocking usually lives in a browser extension that malware and other apps can bypass, and DNS filters rarely show you what is happening live. A machine needs one place that blocks bad domains before a connection starts and cuts the network if that guard is bypassed. Approach: A single Node.js process runs a DNS server on port 53 and an HTTPS proxy on port 5309. Queries are checked against blocklists indexed in SQLite3 and against heuristics (suspicious TLDs such as .zip, .mov, .top and .xyz, and tracker words like ads, track and pixel) before they resolve. It rewrites the system DNS and proxy settings and restores them on shutdown, generates its own certificates for HTTPS inspection, streams every query to a live dashboard over socket.io, and a Windows Firewall kill switch drops outgoing traffic if the proxy goes offline.

chunks.title: SentinelProxy Suite: results and stack
chunks.text: Key result: 53 + 5309 DNS and HTTPS-proxy ports served by one process. Blocklists: millions of domains held in an indexed SQLite3 lookup (design target in the README). Heuristics: suspicious TLDs and tracker substrings blocked before a name resolves. Dashboard: live query log over WebSockets, 12 screenshots in the repo. Packaging: one portable x64 .exe; MIT licence. Stack: Node.js, dns2, http-proxy, SQLite3, Express, socket.io, node-forge. Windows-first: the kill switch and the system hooks use netsh and need an Administrator shell. Inspecting HTTPS means installing its own local certificate authority, so it is meant for machines you own. The README gives no benchmark of lookup speed. Solo product. Code: https://github.com/SahajIVVIX-1/SentinelProxy-Suite

chunks.title: SentinelProxy Suite README: README
chunks.text: 🛡️ Local Proxy & DNS Server Custom Node.js HTTPS Proxy with Live Web Dashboard The Chakhdi Local Proxy & DNS Server is a highly advanced, locally hosted network management system designed for robust traffic control, privacy, and intelligent threat mitigation. Built with a high-performance architecture, it features dynamic ad-blocking, malicious domain filtering (powered by indexed SQLite3 database blocklists), automatic system proxy mapping, and a sleek live metrics dashboard over HTTPS—giving you real-time visual analytics natively coupled with smart threat intelligence.

chunks.title: SentinelProxy Suite README: Key Features
chunks.text: - Advanced HTTPS Proxy: Intercepts, routes, and bumps traffic accurately on port 5309 . - Integrated DNS Server: Listens on port 53 to resolve DNS queries and discard connections to known malicious domains before a connection is even negotiated. - Dynamic Blocklists: Loads millions of domains directly into a fast, in-memory SQLite3 database for zero-latency blocking. - Live Monitoring Dashboard: Real-time Web UI served over HTTPS, using Express and WebSockets ( socket.io ), to let you monitor inbound and outbound queries visually. - Auto-Configuring System Hooks: Modifies the OS network adapters on-the-fly to set the DNS and Proxy to 127.0.0.1 and manages Windows Firewall block rules.

chunks.title: SentinelProxy Suite README: Key Features
chunks.text: Restores configuration automatically on shut down. - Certificate Authority Engine: Uses node-forge for automatic Certificate generation, SSL interception, decryption, and secure key loading. - Network Kill Switch: Instantly enforces Windows Firewall configurations to drop all outgoing internet traffic if the proxy goes offline or is illegally bypassed.

chunks.title: SentinelProxy Suite README: Heuristics & Threat Mitigation Engine
chunks.text: This project implements smart heuristics and robust local filtering to keep your local network clean and secure: - Heuristic Pattern Blocklists: Inspects incoming DNS queries for suspicious top-level domains (such as .zip , .mov , .top , .xyz ) and common tracker substrings ( ads , track , pixel , analytics ) before they are resolved. - SQLite3-Indexed Blocklists: Compiles and indices large hosts blocklists into SQLite3 tables for high-performance, low-latency lookups during active proxying. - Real-Time Telemetry & Log Export: Uses WebSocket-based streaming ( socket.io ) to forward outbound query logs directly to the live dashboard.

chunks.title: SentinelProxy Suite README: Heuristics & Threat Mitigation Engine
chunks.text: This structured query format can easily be integrated into SIEM systems, custom log forwarders, or external analytics engines.

chunks.title: SentinelProxy Suite README: Tech Stack & Architecture
chunks.text: - Node.js : Powers the backend networking and async non-blocking proxying. - dns2 : Core DNS protocol parsing, query management, and customized resolution. - http-proxy : Extremely performant HTTP & HTTPS proxy relay. - socket.io : Real-time bidirectional event-based communication for pushing live metrics directly to the Web Interface. - SQLite3 : Lightning-fast, unbloated data indexing for instant DNS filtering. - node-forge : Certificate and cryptography management toolkit for establishing secure local channels natively.

chunks.title: SentinelProxy Suite README: Troubleshooting
chunks.text: "Kill switch enable failed" / "Command failed: netsh advfirewall" - The network proxy is attempting to set an outbound Windows Firewall safety rule, but access is denied. Please right-click and "Run as Administrator" on your command prompt! "DNS Error: Address in Use" - Another application is likely using Port 53 . Ensure no other DNS processes or localized IIS servers are overlapping the binding connection.
